Raman Analysis of Gypsum and Marble

Start from how chemical bonds vibrate, run PCA and PLS-DA in R, Python and Orange,
map every VIP score and loading back onto a chemical bond — and verify that all three give the same numbers.

43chapters
68questions
3tools
10spectra
664wavenumbers

What this tutorial does

The data are ten Raman spectra: five of gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O) and five of marble (calcite, CaCO3). The goal is to identify the minerals, find the bands that distinguish them, and answer one question: do the wavenumbers a statistical model picks out really correspond to chemical bonds?

Three parallel tracks — R (the pls package), Python (Jupyter, NIPALS written by hand) and Orange (the orange-spectra PLS-DA widget, no code at all). All three do the same thing; Chapter 29 checks item by item that they agree to better than 10-6.

Preprocessing is hand-written throughout Parts 1–6, so that you can see what every step computes. Part 7 switches to the established packages (baseline + prospectr in R, pybaselines + scipy in Python) and quantifies three defaults that raise no error but quietly change the result.

Part 8 is external validation: a published open dataset (J. Cult. Herit. 32, 2018, 355 nm pulsed LIF-Raman) is projected into the model trained here. Getting there means first catching a 46 cm-1 error in the wavelength axis of that data — and the chapter ends with what may and may not be pushed to GitHub.

Who this is for
People who have studied neither vibrational spectroscopy nor chemometrics. Every formula is explained intuitively before any code appears, and every code block can be copied and run as it stands.
Every number and every figure here was produced by actually running r/rock_raman_tutorial.R and python/rock_raman_tutorial.ipynb from this repository.
The most important part comes last
Part 6 shows what happens when a model hands you 100% accuracy and p = 0.0079 while simultaneously awarding second place in the VIP ranking to an instrument artefact that is not in the sample at all.
The advantage of Raman is that this can be caught — because every peak can be checked against the question "what bond is moving there?". That is what this tutorial is really about.
How to use it
Mark each chapter done with the button at its foot; every part ends with a short quiz. Progress is kept in your browser (localStorage) and survives closing the page. There is a dashboard at the end that exports your record as CSV, and every code block has a one-click copy button.

Part 1 — Chemistry: why 1008 and 1086Seven chapters. No code, but everything downstream depends on it

1. Raman looks at chemical bonds vibrating

Shine a laser on a stone and almost all the light bounces back unchanged. But roughly one photon in a hundred million exchanges a packet of energy with a chemical bond before it leaves — and that packet is exactly the energy of one vibration of that bond.

Plot those energy differences and you have a Raman spectrum: the x-axis is the Raman shift (the wavenumber difference between incident and scattered light, in cm-1) and the y-axis is intensity.

The key property is this: the vibrational frequency of a chemical group is set by its bond strength and the masses of its atoms, and is nearly independent of what sits next to it or which laser you used. Sulfate stretches symmetrically at about 1000 cm-1 whether it sits in gypsum, anhydrite or barite. Carbonate does so at about 1080 cm-1 in calcite, aragonite or dolomite alike.

This is the answer to "can a peak be mapped to a chemical bond?"
Yes, and the mapping is one-to-one.
A Raman peak is not a statistical feature. It is a physical quantity: each peak corresponds to one specific normal mode of vibration.

That gives Raman an unusual position in chemometrics — your PCA loadings and PLS-DA VIP scores can be checked one by one. If the model says a wavenumber matters, you can look it up and ask "what bond is moving there?". If you cannot answer, that variable is probably not to be trusted.

This is a luxury most machine-learning applications do not have. Part 6 shows how to use it to catch the model making a mistake.

2. Why the symmetric stretch is the strongest Raman band

Infrared absorption responds to changes in dipole moment. Raman responds to changes in polarisability (α). That single word decides why the two techniques produce spectra that look nothing alike.

Raman scattering intensity is proportional to (∂α/∂Q)² — how much the ease of deforming the electron cloud changes during the vibration.

Symmetric stretch (ν1)
Every bond lengthens and shortens together. The whole ion breathes in and out, so the electron-cloud volume changes as much as it possibly can → largest ∂α/∂Q → strongest in Raman.
And because it is symmetric, the dipole moment does not change → often invisible in the infrared.
Antisymmetric stretch (ν3)
One side lengthens while the other shortens. Volume barely changes, so α barely changes → weak in Raman.
But the dipole moment swings → strong in the infrared.

So the pattern you will see in this dataset has a reason behind it: gypsum's 1008 (ν1) is tall and sharp while 1135 (ν3) is barely visible; calcite's 1086 (ν1) is tall and sharp while 1435 (ν3) is barely visible. Measure the same samples by FTIR and the intensities invert.

A practical corollary
ν1 is the only totally symmetric mode, and its scattered light keeps the polarisation of the incident beam (depolarisation ratio ρ < 0.75).
Some instruments can therefore use a polariser to pick ν1 out and suppress everything else — an experimental way to settle "is this really ν1?".

3. The four modes of sulfate, SO₄²⁻

SO42- is a regular tetrahedron (Td). Five atoms give 3×5−6 = 9 vibrational degrees of freedom, grouped into four modes:

ModeSymmetryMotionWavenumber (cm⁻¹)Raman
ν1A1all four S–O stretch together (breathing)1008strongest
ν2Esymmetric bend (O–S–O angle)413 / 493medium
ν3F2antisymmetric stretch1135weak
ν4F2antisymmetric bend620 / 670weak

Why does ν2 have two numbers? A free SO42- ion is a perfect tetrahedron and ν2 is doubly degenerate (E — two modes at the same energy). Inside the gypsum crystal the environment around the sulfate is not perfectly symmetric, so the degeneracy is lifted and one band splits into two. The same happens to ν4 (triply degenerate F2), which splits into 620 and 670.

This is called site symmetry lowering. It is not noise — the size of the splitting carries information about the local environment.

Gypsum also carries two waters
CaSO4·2H2O. Those two waters of crystallisation stretch at 3405 and 3494 cm⁻¹ (two bands, because the two water molecules sit in different environments).
Free water stretches at 3657/3756; hydrogen bonding in the lattice drags it down by more than two hundred wavenumbers. The stronger the hydrogen bond, the bigger the drop — a standard way of characterising hydrous minerals.

In this dataset the 3400 region is too weak to use. Getting it would need a separate measurement targeted at the high-wavenumber region.

Dehydration writes itself onto ν₁

MineralFormulaν1 (cm⁻¹)
gypsumCaSO4·2H2O1008
bassaniteCaSO4·0.5H2O1015
anhydriteCaSO41017

As water leaves, the sulfate's surroundings stiffen, the force constant rises and ν1 moves up. Seven to nine wavenumbers apart means a different mineral — do not write "gypsum" the moment you see something in the low 1000s.
There is a practical warning here too: too much laser power will bake gypsum into bassanite while you watch, and you will see 1008 creep towards 1015 on screen.

4. The four modes of carbonate — and the one that vanishes

CO32- is a planar triangle (D3h). Four atoms give 3×4−6 = 6 degrees of freedom:

ModeSymmetryMotionWavenumber (cm⁻¹)Raman
ν1A1′all three C–O stretch together1086strongest
ν2A2″carbon moves out of the plane872invisible
ν3E′antisymmetric stretch1435very weak
ν4E′in-plane bend712medium
Why 872 does not exist in a Raman spectrum
This is not weakness. It is forbidden by symmetry.

For a vibration to be Raman active its symmetry must match one of the components of the polarisability tensor. In the D3h point group the Raman-active representations are A1′, E′ and E″ only. ν2 belongs to A2″, which is not on that list → Raman intensity is strictly zero.

A2″ happens to correspond to a dipole change along z → very strong in the infrared. So 872 cm⁻¹ is the best FTIR band for identifying carbonates and will never appear in a Raman spectrum.

This is the textbook example of Raman and FTIR being complementary: neither is better, they see different things.

You can verify it yourself: look at the figure in Chapter 7 — the marble spectrum has nothing at 872 cm-1, and it is pure calcite. That is not a problem with the data.

5. Why 1008 and 1086 are 78 cm⁻¹ apart

Both are symmetric stretches of an oxyanion. Why is carbonate 78 cm-1 higher?

Start with one key fact: in the ν1 mode the central atom does not move at all.

For both a tetrahedral XY4 and a planar XY3, the totally symmetric stretch moves every Y atom radially in and out together. Perfect symmetry keeps the centre of mass fixed, so the central X atom stays put. The effective mass is therefore the mass of oxygen — identical for sulfate and carbonate.

ν ∝ √(k / mO) mO identical → the difference is entirely in k

k is the X–O stretching force constant. C–O is short (about 1.28 Å) and of high bond order; S–O is longer (about 1.49 Å) and comparatively soft. C–O is stiffer than S–O, so carbonate's ν1 sits higher.

Working backwards: (1086/1008)² = 1.16, so the effective C–O force constant is about 16% larger.

Why this deserves a whole chapter
Because it turns "1008 vs 1086" from two numbers to memorise into a result you can derive.

Students forget which is which. They do not forget "C–O is stiffer than S–O, so carbonate is on the right".
And the reasoning extrapolates: phosphate PO43- has ν1 at 960 (P–O is softer than S–O), nitrate NO3- at 1050. Same logic, no table needed.

6. Lattice modes: where 282 comes from

The four modes above are internal to the ion — take the carbonate out of the crystal and drop it in water and they are still there.

But calcite also shows clear peaks at 156 and 282 cm-1, and those are external (lattice) modes: the whole CO32- group moving as a rigid body against the Ca2+ ions.

WavenumberTypeMotion
156T (translational)whole carbonate group oscillating against Ca
282L (librational)whole carbonate group rocking in place
Why lattice modes discriminate better than internal modes
Because they reflect crystal structure, not just chemical composition.

The classic case: calcite and aragonite are both CaCO₃, with ν1 at 1086 and 1085 respectively — one wavenumber apart, indistinguishable at normal resolution.
But the lattice region is completely different: calcite 156 / 282, aragonite 152 / 206. Obvious at a glance.

So identifying "marble" cannot rest on 1086 alone. The low-wavenumber region (150–300) is mandatory — and that is why Chapter 9 crops at 150 rather than 400.

Incidentally, in this dataset marble's 282 peak (135.8) is almost as tall as 1086 (143.0) — but in a reference calcite spectrum 1086 should be clearly stronger. That is an instrument response problem, dealt with in Chapter 33.

7. Master table: every peak and its bond

Print this. Every time a loading or VIP score points at a wavenumber, come back and look it up.

Wavenumber (cm⁻¹)MineralModeWhat is movingRaman intensity
156calcitelattice TCO3 rigid-body translation against Camedium
282calcitelattice LCO3 rigid-body librationmedium-strong
413 / 493gypsumSO4 ν2O–S–O bending (degeneracy lifted by the lattice)medium
620 / 670gypsumSO4 ν4antisymmetric bendweak
712calciteCO3 ν4in-plane bendmedium
872calciteCO3 ν2C out of plane — Raman forbidden, FTIR only0
1008gypsumSO4 ν1four S–O breathing togetherstrongest · diagnostic
1086calciteCO3 ν1three C–O breathing togetherstrongest · diagnostic
1135gypsumSO4 ν3antisymmetric stretchweak
1435calciteCO3 ν3antisymmetric stretchvery weak
3405 / 3494gypsumH2OO–H stretch of the waters of crystallisationweak (not captured here)
419neither—instrument artefact (Chapter 30)—
The order in which to read a spectrum
1. Look at 1000–1100 first: is it 1008 or 1086? → sulfate or carbonate
2. Then the lattice region 150–300: confirm calcite rather than aragonite, gypsum rather than anhydrite
3. Finally, look for bands appearing where they should not → an artefact, or a second phase

Only after those three steps are you entitled to start doing statistics.

Part 1 · Quiz

Q1.Raman scattering intensity is proportional to the change in what?
Dipole moment
Polarisability
Bond length
Molecular mass
Explanation: Raman intensity ∝ (∂α/∂Q)². Infrared absorption is the one that responds to dipole moment. That one difference is why the same sample gives completely different-looking Raman and FTIR spectra.
Q2.Why is the symmetric stretch ν₁ usually the strongest Raman band?
It has the highest energy
All bonds breathe together, so the electron-cloud volume change and ∂α/∂Q are maximal
It is the only allowed mode
Because its wavenumber is largest
Explanation: The totally symmetric breathing mode changes the polarisability as much as possible. Being symmetric, it leaves the dipole moment unchanged, which is why it is often invisible in the infrared.
Q3.Why does gypsum's SO₄ ν₂ split into 413 and 493?
There are two kinds of sulfate present
The crystal site symmetry is lower than a perfect tetrahedron, lifting the degeneracy
It is an artefact of insufficient resolution
They are two different minerals
Explanation: A free SO₄²⁻ has a doubly degenerate ν₂ (E). The lattice environment is not perfectly symmetric, so the degeneracy is lifted. The size of the splitting carries structural information.
Q4.Why is calcite's ν₂ (872 cm⁻¹) absent from the Raman spectrum?
The signal is too weak and buried in noise
Symmetry forbidden — A₂″ is not among the Raman-active representations of D₃ₕ
It is hidden under the shoulder of 1086
It is outside the detector range
Explanation: Strictly zero, not weak. The Raman-active representations of D₃ₕ are A₁′, E′ and E″ only; ν₂ is A₂″, which corresponds to a dipole change along z → very strong in FTIR, zero in Raman. The textbook example of complementarity.
Q5.Why is carbonate's ν₁ (1086) higher than sulfate's ν₁ (1008)?
Carbon is lighter than sulfur, so the reduced mass is smaller
The effective mass is oxygen in both cases; the difference comes entirely from C–O being a stiffer bond than S–O
The carbonate ion has a smaller radius
Because carbonate is planar
Explanation: In the totally symmetric ν₁ mode the central atom does not move, so the effective mass is oxygen for both. Therefore ν ∝ √k and the difference is purely the force constant: (1086/1008)² ≈ 1.16, about 16% stiffer.
Q6.Calcite and aragonite are both CaCO₃ with ν₁ only 1 cm⁻¹ apart. How do you tell them apart?
By the position of ν₄
By the lattice region: calcite 156/282, aragonite 152/206
By peak height ratios
By the water bands
Explanation: Lattice (external) modes reflect crystal structure rather than composition, so they discriminate best between polymorphs. This is also why the crop must start at 150 rather than 400.
Q7.Gypsum 1008, bassanite 1015, anhydrite 1017. Why does the wavenumber rise as water leaves?
The mass decreases
Without water the sulfate's surroundings stiffen, raising the S–O force constant
The crystal expands
It is measurement error
Explanation: A practical warning: too much laser power bakes gypsum into bassanite while you watch, and you see 1008 creeping towards 1015. Look carefully at which one you actually have.
Q8.Peaks map one-to-one onto chemical bonds. Why does that matter for PCA and PLS-DA?
It lets you skip preprocessing
The variables the model flags as important can be verified individually; a variable with no chemical meaning should be treated as suspect
It removes the need for cross-validation
It increases the sample size
Explanation: In most machine-learning applications you cannot check whether the features a model uses make sense. In Raman you can — and Part 6 uses exactly that to catch the model relying on an instrument artefact.

One row = one spectrum, one column = one wavenumber. From the third column on, the column name is the wavenumber — so VIP tables come out already labelled in cm⁻¹.

10 samples, 664 variables
Variables outnumber samples 66 to one. This is the p ≫ n regime.
The consequence: any flexible model can separate the data perfectly, even with randomly shuffled labels. So "100% accuracy" is not by itself evidence of anything.
Chapter 32 quantifies exactly how much.

9. Cropping to 150–1800

R
sel <- wn0 >= 150 & wn0 <= 1800
wn  <- wn0[sel]
X   <- X0[, sel]
length(wn)     # 664
Python
sel = (wn0 >= 150) & (wn0 <= 1800)
wn, X = wn0[sel], X0[:, sel]
len(wn)        # 664

Three reasons:

  1. Lower bound 150. Below that is the edge of the laser rejection filter, which is instrument signal. But you must not cut at 400 either — calcite's lattice bands at 156 and 282 live there, and they are the only way to tell calcite from aragonite (Chapter 6).
  2. Upper bound 1800. The waters-of-crystallisation region (3400/3494) is too weak in this dataset; keeping 1200 columns of pure noise only dilutes the variance PCA has to work with.
  3. Order matters: crop first, then baseline. ALS fits globally. Leave the steep edge at 77 cm-1 in place and it drags the start of the baseline up, which shifts the whole 200–500 region with it.
Crop limits belong in the methods section
Where you crop changes the direction of the principal components and the order of the VIP ranking. This is a researcher degree of freedom: state it, and do not go back and adjust it later because the result looks nicer.

10. ALS baseline

In one sentence: find a curve that is as smooth as possible while hugging the data from below. Smoothness is enforced by penalising the second difference (curvature); hugging from below comes from asymmetric weights — points above the current baseline get only 1% weight, because those are the peaks.

R
als <- function(y, lambda = 1e4, p = 0.01, niter = 15) {
  m  <- length(y)
  D  <- diff(Diagonal(m), differences = 2)   # 2nd-difference matrix = curvature
  DD <- lambda * crossprod(D)
  w  <- rep(1, m)
  for (i in 1:niter) {
    W <- Diagonal(x = w)
    z <- as.numeric(solve(W + DD, w * y))    # weighted smooth solution
    w <- p * (y > z) + (1 - p) * (y <= z)    # down-weight points above (peaks)
  }
  z
}
Python
from scipy import sparse
from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve

def als(y, lam=1e4, p=0.01, niter=15):
    m = len(y)
    D = sparse.diags([1., -2., 1.], [0, 1, 2], shape=(m - 2, m), format="csc")
    DD = lam * (D.T @ D)
    w = np.ones(m)
    for _ in range(niter):
        W = sparse.diags(w, 0, format="csc")
        z = spsolve((W + DD).tocsc(), w * y)
        w = p * (y > z) + (1 - p) * (y <= z)
    return z
ParameterToo largeToo small
lambda (smoothness)baseline too stiff; broad fluorescence humps survive and get mistaken for wide peaksbaseline too flexible; it burrows into the peak feet and eats real signal
p (asymmetry)baseline rides up, peak heights underestimatedbaseline hugs too low, noise minima treated as baseline
Why 1e4 for this dataset
Chosen after trying three orders of magnitude. 1e5 was too stiff; 1e3 started shaving the foot of the 1008 band.
The test is simple: plot it. The baseline should hug the data where there are no peaks and pass smoothly beneath the peaks where there are.
Do not trust anyone who tells you a default is always right — the value depends on your instrument, your sample and how much it fluoresces.

11. Savitzky–Golay

Take a small window around each point, fit a low-order polynomial by least squares, and replace the point with the polynomial's value at the centre. Better than a moving average because it does not flatten peaks.

R
sg <- function(y, w = 9, poly = 3, deriv = 0) {
  hw <- (w - 1) / 2; k <- -hw:hw
  A  <- outer(k, 0:poly, "^")          # Vandermonde matrix
  C  <- solve(crossprod(A), t(A))      # least-squares solution
  cf <- C[deriv + 1, ] * factorial(deriv)
  n  <- length(y)
  yp <- c(rep(y[1], hw), y, rep(y[n], hw))   # pad both ends with the end values
  sapply(1:n, function(i) sum(cf * yp[i:(i + w - 1)]))
}
Python
def sg(y, w=9, poly=3, deriv=0):
    hw = (w - 1) // 2
    k  = np.arange(-hw, hw + 1)
    A  = np.vander(k, poly + 1, increasing=True)
    C  = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A, A.T)
    cf = C[deriv] * math.factorial(deriv)
    yp = np.r_[np.repeat(y[0], hw), y, np.repeat(y[-1], hw)]
    return np.array([cf @ yp[i:i + w] for i in range(len(y))])
Why not just use scipy.signal.savgol_filter?
Because the edge handling differs. scipy defaults to mode='interp' (polynomial extrapolation); the R version here pads with the end values.
The difference affects only the four outermost points — but if you want R and Python to agree exactly, they have to be written the same way.

Mismatched defaults like this are the single most common cross-language reproducibility trap. They never raise an error; they just leave the two sides slightly different, and then you spend three hours looking for the cause.

Choose parameters by how wide your peaks are. Here the FWHM is roughly 10–15 points, so the window must be clearly narrower than the peak. w=9, poly=3 is the field default.

deriv=1 gives the first derivative. A constant background differentiates to zero, so the first derivative removes additive baseline offsets automatically; a peak turns into a positive–negative S shape whose zero crossing is the original peak centre. The cost is amplified noise, which is why you must smooth before differentiating (SG does both in one pass).

12. SNV and the four preprocessing variants

R
snv <- function(y) (y - mean(y)) / sd(y)
Python
def snv(y):
    return (y - y.mean()) / y.std(ddof=1)    # ddof=1 to match R's sd()
The ddof=1 trap
numpy's std() defaults to the population standard deviation (divide by n); R's sd() is the sample standard deviation (divide by n−1).
With 664 points the difference is tiny — but it will put R and Python apart in the fourth decimal place, which is small enough that you assume floating-point error and large enough that it isn't.

Four datasets, compared at every subsequent step:

R
BASE <- t(apply(X, 1, als))        # the fluorescence baseline itself
Xbl  <- t(apply(X - BASE, 1, sg))  # baseline-corrected + smoothed  <- main analysis
Xsnv <- t(apply(Xbl,  1, snv))     # + SNV
Xd1  <- t(apply(Xsnv, 1, sg, deriv = 1))   # + first derivative
SETS <- list(Raw = X, Baseline = Xbl, SNV = Xsnv, `SNV+D1` = Xd1)

Look at panel B. Green (gypsum) grows a sharp peak at 1008; blue (marble) grows a sharp peak at 1086. The mineral identification is already done at this point. Everything that follows — PCA, PLS-DA — exists to turn that judgement into something quantitative, repeatable, and able to cope with hundreds of spectra.

13. Why all three tools share one preprocessing file

This tutorial preprocesses once, saves the result as data/rock_preprocessed.csv and .tab, and has R, Python and Orange all read the same file.

1Preprocess in R or Pythoncrop → ALS → SG, export CSV and Orange .tab
↓
2All three read the same matrixR · Python · Orange
↓
3Each runs PCA / PLS-DAthe numbers must match — verified in Chapter 29

Two reasons:

  1. Pedagogically: if each tool preprocessed independently and produced different numbers, a student could not tell whether the difference came from the tool or from the preprocessing. Fix the preprocessing and the only remaining difference is the algorithm itself — which turns out to be the same algorithm.
  2. Practically: Orange's Spectroscopy add-on has a Preprocess Spectra widget and can certainly do baselines and smoothing. But its ALS implementation, parameter names and edge handling will not be identical to yours. To compare tools you must first hold everything else constant.
So where should preprocessing actually live?
Wherever you need to repeat it.
・One-off exploration → drag it together in Orange, fastest
・A hundred samples, re-run monthly → an R or Python script
・Going to publication → a script, with the parameters in the methods section

These are not in conflict: Orange to look, scripts to deliver.

Part 2 · Quiz

Q1.Why crop at 150 rather than 400 cm⁻¹?
There is no signal below 150
Calcite's lattice bands at 156/282 live there and are the only way to distinguish calcite from aragonite
To make the point count a round number
Convention
Explanation: Lattice modes reflect crystal structure. Calcite and aragonite differ by 1 cm⁻¹ in ν₁ and can only be told apart by 156/282 vs 152/206. Cut at 400 and you lose that forever.
Q2.Why crop before baseline correction rather than after?
It runs faster
ALS fits globally; leaving the steep edges in place drags the whole baseline out of shape
Cropping changes the wavenumber calibration
The order does not matter
Explanation: The filter cut-off edge at 77 cm⁻¹ pulls the start of the baseline up, which shifts the entire 200–500 region.
Q3.What happens if the ALS lambda is too small?
The baseline is too stiff and broad humps survive
The baseline is too flexible and burrows into the peak feet, eating real signal
Peak positions shift
It fails to converge
Explanation: Too large is the opposite — residual humps get mistaken for broad peaks. The only real test is to plot it and check that the baseline passes smoothly beneath the peaks.
Q4.Why does this tutorial hand-write SG instead of using scipy.signal.savgol_filter?
The scipy implementation has a bug
The edge handling differs (scipy defaults to interp, this pads with end values); matching R exactly requires writing it the same way
savgol_filter cannot compute derivatives
For speed
Explanation: Mismatched defaults never raise an error. They just leave the two sides slightly different — small enough that you assume floating-point error.
Q5.How does numpy's std() differ from R's sd()?
No difference
numpy defaults to ddof=0 (divide by n); R uses the sample SD (divide by n−1)
numpy is more precise
R drops NAs automatically and numpy does not
Explanation: For SNV you must write y.std(ddof=1) to match R. This is one of the most common cross-language reproducibility traps.
Q6.What does a first derivative do to an additive baseline offset?
Amplifies it
Removes it automatically (a constant differentiates to zero), at the cost of amplified noise
Nothing
Converts it to a multiplicative offset
Explanation: Which is why you must smooth before differentiating. SG does both in one pass — that is why it beats 'moving average then diff'.
Q7.Why does this tutorial share one preprocessed file across R, Python and Orange?
To save disk space
To hold everything else constant so the only remaining difference is the algorithm; otherwise you cannot tell tool differences from preprocessing differences
Orange cannot preprocess
CSV is faster
Explanation: Orange's Spectroscopy add-on can certainly preprocess, but its ALS implementation and parameter names will not be identical to a hand-written one. To compare tools, first fix everything else.
Q8.10 samples, 664 variables. What does 100% accuracy mean in that setting?
The model is good
By itself, nothing — under p ≫ n even shuffled labels can reach high accuracy, so it must be validated separately
The data are corrupted
The number of components should be reduced
Explanation: Variables outnumber samples 66 to one. Chapter 32 quantifies exactly what randomly shuffled labels can achieve on this dataset.

Part 3 — RFive chapters. One add-on package: pls

14. Setup and reading the data

Shell
install.packages("pls")   # the only one you need. Matrix ships with R
R
suppressMessages({ library(Matrix); library(pls) })
set.seed(20260814)

d   <- read.csv("../data/rock_raman_2class_raw.csv", check.names = FALSE)
wn  <- as.numeric(colnames(d)[-(1:2)])
X   <- as.matrix(d[, -(1:2)]); rownames(X) <- d$ID
grp <- factor(d$type); ids <- d$ID; lev <- levels(grp)
Three details worth memorising
check.names = FALSE — without it R rewrites the column name 150.004 as X150.004, as.numeric() then returns all NA, and nothing raises an error. You simply get a blank plot.

as.matrix() — data frames and matrices are different objects in R, and apply() and t() behave differently on them.

factor() — the level order determines the dummy-variable column order, and therefore whether the class name that which.max picks out is the right one.

One more idiom that recurs throughout:

R
Xbl <- t(apply(X, 1, function(y) sg(y - als(y))))
#      ^ this t() is not decorative

apply(X, 1, f) operates row-wise but stacks each return value as a column, so the result is transposed. Forget the t() and every dimension downstream is wrong.

15. PCA

R
pc <- prcomp(Xbl, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
ve <- 100 * pc$sdev^2 / sum(pc$sdev^2)

center = TRUE is mandatory — the definition of PCA presumes centred data.

scale. = FALSE — for spectra you generally do not standardise each wavenumber column. This is the opposite of the usual advice for tabular data, and the reason is that all columns share a unit (counts) while most of them contain nothing but noise. Standardising promotes a pure-noise wavenumber to the same importance as the 1086 band, and PC1 ends up describing noise.

PreprocessingPC1PC2PC3
Raw85.8%10.7%1.0%
Baseline86.3%4.4%3.5%
SNV86.1%5.2%3.3%
SNV+D176.8%5.7%4.9%

Read a scree plot by looking for the elbow: PC1 86.3%, PC2 drops to 4.4%. Separating k groups requires at most k−1 dimensions, so with two groups a dominant PC1 is the expected result, not an anomaly.

Convex hulls, not confidence ellipses
Five points per group. Fitting a 95% confidence ellipse means estimating a covariance matrix from five points, and the size of the resulting ellipse is essentially arbitrary — drawing one implies a statistical guarantee that is not there.
chull() is honest: it is exactly "the range these five points cover", and it promises nothing more.

16. Loading plots: translating a PC back into chemistry

A score plot tells you who resembles whom. A loading plot tells you which peak is responsible. Reporting the first without the second is the most common shortcut in this field.

R
L <- pc$rotation[, 1]
o <- order(-abs(L))[1:10]
data.frame(wn = round(wn[o], 1), loading = round(L[o], 4),
           side = ifelse(L[o] > 0, "calcite", "gypsum"))
Output
     wn loading    side
 1086.0  0.2274 calcite     <- CO3 v1     * real signal
 1083.6  0.2135 calcite     <- shoulder of 1086
 1088.5  0.2123 calcite     <- shoulder of 1086
  419.2 -0.2115  gypsum     <- INSTRUMENT ARTEFACT
  283.5  0.2072 calcite     <- lattice L  *
  286.4  0.2051 calcite     <- lattice L  *
  422.1 -0.2006  gypsum     <- artefact
  416.4 -0.1999  gypsum     <- artefact + SO4 v2 overlap
  280.6  0.1926 calcite     <- lattice L  *
  289.4  0.1861 calcite     <- lattice L  *

Now you can write a sentence like this:

PC1 (86.3%) is built from positive loadings on the calcite ν1 (1086 cm-1), lattice (282) and ν4 (712) bands, and negative loadings on the gypsum ν1 (1008) and ν2 (413) bands, separating the two groups completely.

— rather than merely "the two groups are well separated (PC1 = 86.3%)".

But look at rank 4
419.2 is not a chemical signal. Chapter 30 shows that it appears on the calcite samples, which have no vibrational mode there.
PCA has no way of knowing this. It is honestly reporting "there is a lot of variance here." Deciding whether that variance is chemistry is your job.
This is why Part 1 cannot be skipped — without it you would not even know what to be suspicious of.

17. PLS-DA and VIP

PLS is a regression method. To classify with it, encode the classes as a 0/1 dummy matrix Y, regress it on X with PLS2, and predict by taking whichever output column is largest.

R
Ydum    <- function(g) { m <- model.matrix(~ g - 1); colnames(m) <- levels(g); m }
fitpls  <- function(X, g, nc) plsr(Ydum(g) ~ X, ncomp = nc,
                                   method = "oscorespls", scale = FALSE)
predcls <- function(m, Xn, lev, nc) {
  pr <- predict(m, newdata = Xn, ncomp = nc)
  factor(lev[apply(matrix(pr, ncol = length(lev)), 1, which.max)], levels = lev)
}
mod <- fitpls(Xbl, grp, 4)
pls::explvar(mod)     # Comp1 86.30   Comp2 3.98   Comp3 1.61   Comp4 3.03
Use method = "oscorespls", not "simpls"
oscorespls (orthogonal scores) is the classic NIPALS PLS2 — the same algorithm orange-spectra's plsda_fit() uses, which is why the numbers agree.

simpls is faster but does not return loading.weights, which the VIP formula needs. You will get Error in colSums(W^2) : 'x' must be an array of at least two dimensions.

VIP

VIPj = √( p · Σa[ ssya · (wja/‖wa‖)² ] / Σa ssya )

where ssya = (ta′ta)(qa′qa) is the Y variance explained by component a. The conventional threshold is VIP > 1, because the mean of the squared VIP scores is exactly 1 — so "greater than 1" means "above average contribution".

R
vip <- function(m, nc) {
  W  <- m$loading.weights[, 1:nc, drop = FALSE]
  T  <- m$scores[,          1:nc, drop = FALSE]
  Q  <- m$Yloadings[,       1:nc, drop = FALSE]
  SS <- colSums(Q^2) * colSums(T^2)
  Wn <- sweep(W, 2, sqrt(colSums(W^2)), "/")
  sqrt(nrow(W) * rowSums(sweep(Wn^2, 2, SS, "*")) / sum(SS))
}
V <- vip(mod, 2)
sum(V > 1)      # 55  of 664
#cm⁻¹VIPAssignment
11086.05.718calcite CO3 ν1 ★
2419.25.574instrument artefact
31083.65.373shoulder of 1086
41088.55.338shoulder of 1086
5422.15.310instrument artefact
6283.55.249calcite lattice L ★
7416.45.244artefact + gypsum ν2 overlap
8286.45.200calcite lattice L ★
111009.34.581gypsum SO4 ν1 ★

18. Cross-validation and the exact permutation test

Leave-one-out cross-validation

R
loocv <- function(M, g, ncmax = 4) {
  n <- nrow(M); res <- matrix(NA, n, ncmax)
  for (i in 1:n) {
    # the point: rebuild the model, not just the prediction, on every fold
    m <- fitpls(M[-i, , drop = FALSE], factor(g[-i], levels = lev), ncmax)
    for (a in 1:ncmax) res[i, a] <- as.character(predcls(m, M[i, , drop = FALSE], lev, a))
  }
  apply(res, 2, function(p) mean(p == as.character(g)))
}
Output
  Raw       1LV=0.900  2LV=1.000  3LV=1.000  4LV=1.000
  Baseline  1LV=1.000  2LV=1.000  3LV=1.000  4LV=1.000
  SNV       1LV=1.000  2LV=1.000  3LV=1.000  4LV=1.000
  SNV+D1    1LV=1.000  2LV=1.000  3LV=1.000  4LV=1.000
The classic fatal mistake in cross-validation
Selecting variables or tuning parameters on the whole dataset, and only then splitting off the validation set.

For example: pick "the 50 wavenumbers with the highest VIP" using all 10 samples, then run leave-one-out on those 50. The held-out sample's information has already leaked into the variable selection, and the accuracy is badly inflated.

The rule is simple: every step that touches Y must live inside the cross-validation loop. Baseline correction and SNV act on one spectrum at a time and never see Y, so they can stay outside.

The exact permutation test

The sample is small enough that random permutation is wasteful. Five versus five gives only C(10,5) = 252 possible label assignments — enumerate all of them and the p-value is exact.

R
cmb  <- combn(10, 5)                     # 252 columns
accs <- apply(cmb, 2, function(idx) {
  gg <- factor(ifelse(1:10 %in% idx, lev[1], lev[2]), levels = lev)
  mean(sapply(1:10, function(i) {
    m <- fitpls(Xbl[-i, , drop = FALSE], factor(gg[-i], levels = lev), 2)
    as.character(predcls(m, Xbl[i, , drop = FALSE], lev, 2))
  }) == as.character(gg))
})
sum(accs >= obs) / length(accs)          # 2/252 = 0.0079
Observed accuracy1.000
Mean under shuffled labels0.426
Maximum under shuffled labels1.000
p-value2 / 252 = 0.0079
Only two assignments reach 100%
The true labelling, and the one with both labels swapped — the model simply learns the reversed mapping and scores identically.

So p = 2/252 = 0.0079 is the floor for a five-versus-five design. It cannot go lower.
However perfect your signal, you cannot obtain p < 0.0079.

This is something to know while designing the experiment, not after analysing it. For p < 0.001 you need at least six per group (C(12,6) = 924, so 2/924 = 0.0022).

Q1.What happens if you forget check.names = FALSE in read.csv?
It throws an error
The column name 150.004 becomes X150.004, as.numeric returns all NA, and nothing raises an error
The file will not load
Values get rounded
Explanation: The silence is the problem. You get a vector of NAs for your wavenumbers, a blank plot, and no clue why.
Q2.Why is preprocessing written as t(apply(X, 1, f))?
For speed
apply stacks each return value as a column, so the result comes out transposed
t() is cosmetic
The t() is unnecessary
Explanation: apply(X, 1, f) works row-wise but transposes the output. Without t() you get 664×10 instead of 10×664 and every dimension downstream is wrong.
Q3.Why set scale. = FALSE for PCA on spectra?
It is faster
All columns share a unit and most contain only noise; standardising promotes noise wavenumbers to the same importance as the main bands
prcomp does not support scaling
SNV has already been applied
Explanation: This is the opposite of the usual advice for tabular data. The exception is when you combine variables from different instruments with different units — then you do need to scale.
Q4.Why use method = "oscorespls" rather than "simpls" for PLS-DA?
It is more accurate
simpls does not return loading.weights, so VIP cannot be computed
simpls does not support two classes
oscorespls is faster
Explanation: oscorespls is NIPALS PLS2, the same algorithm orange-spectra's plsda_fit uses — which is why the numbers match. With simpls you get 'x must be an array of at least two dimensions'.
Q5.Where does the VIP > 1 threshold come from?
A rule of thumb with no theoretical basis
The mean of the squared VIP scores is exactly 1, so 'greater than 1' means 'above average contribution'
A critical value from the t distribution
It is the pls package default
Explanation: It follows directly from the definition, so the threshold means the same thing on any dataset. But it only says 'above average' — it says nothing about chemical meaning.
Q6.VIP ranks 2, 5 and 7 are 419.2 / 422.1 / 416.4. What does that tell you?
That region is an important mineral feature
The model is placing substantial weight on an instrument artefact
More components are needed
The VIP formula is wrong
Explanation: Calcite has no mode at 419, yet the marble spectra show one. A high VIP means 'the model used it', not 'it has chemical meaning'.
Q7.What is the classic fatal mistake in cross-validation?
Too few folds
Selecting variables or tuning on the whole dataset before splitting off the validation set (information leakage)
Not setting a random seed
Too small a sample
Explanation: Rule: every step that touches Y goes inside the CV loop. Baseline correction and SNV act per spectrum and never see Y, so they can stay outside.
Q8.For a five-versus-five design, what is the lowest possible permutation p-value, and why?
0, it can approach zero
2/252 = 0.0079, because both the true labelling and its complete swap reach 100%
1/252 = 0.0040
0.05
Explanation: Swapping both labels makes the model learn the reversed mapping and score identically. For p < 0.001 you need at least six per group (2/924 = 0.0022). Know this before you design the experiment.

20. Loading and preprocessing

Python
import math, numpy as np, pandas as pd

d   = pd.read_csv("../data/rock_raman_2class_raw.csv")

X.shape        # (10, 664)

The three preprocessing functions were listed side by side with their R equivalents in Chapters 10–12. What matters here is the check:

Python
BASE = np.array([als(y) for y in X])
Xbl  = np.array([sg(y) for y in X - BASE])

ref  = pd.read_csv("../data/rock_preprocessed.csv")   # produced by the R script

Output
max |difference| between R and Python = 5.026e-07

The residual is of order 10-7 — exactly the size of R's rounding to six decimal places on export. The two preprocessing pipelines are the same thing.

Make this a habit
Every time you move data between tools, the first thing you do is compare a known intermediate result. Do not wait until the end to discover the numbers do not match.
One line of np.abs(a-b).max() can save you three hours.

21. PCA by SVD

sklearn.decomposition.PCA works perfectly well, but hand-writing the SVD takes three lines and every step is visible:

Python
def pca(M):
    Xc = M - M.mean(axis=0)                       # centre
    U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)
    ve = 100 * S**2 / (S**2).sum()
    return U * S, Vt, ve        # scores, loadings (one PC per row), % variance

scores, load, ve = pca(Xbl)
PCA is SVD
Take the singular value decomposition of the centred matrix, Xc = U S VT:
・each column of V is a loading (a principal component direction)
・U S gives the scores (where each sample sits in the new coordinates)
・S² is proportional to the variance each component explains

Once you see this, "what is PCA actually doing" stops being mysterious — it finds an orthogonal basis that maximises variance in order.

Note that load has shape (664, 664) with one PC per row, while R's pc$rotation has one PC per column. Watch for that transposition when comparing across languages.

Also: the sign of a loading is arbitrary. SVD can flip a column of V and the corresponding column of U together and the result is exactly equivalent. So align signs before comparing:

Python
s = np.sign(load[0] @ R["PC1"].to_numpy())    # are the two the same way round?
np.abs(load[0] * s - R["PC1"].to_numpy()).max()

22. PLS-DA: NIPALS line by line

This section is the core of the notebook. It is the same implementation as plsda_fit() in orangespectra/core.py — the code that actually runs when you click in the Orange widget.

Step 1: classes become dummy variables

Python
classes = sorted(set(labels))                 # ['gypsum', 'marble']
Y = np.zeros((n, len(classes)))
for i, l in enumerate(labels):
    Y[i, classes.index(l)] = 1.0

Step 2: centre (but do not scale)

Python
x_mean, y_mean = X.mean(axis=0), Y.mean(axis=0)
Xc, Yc = X - x_mean, Y - y_mean

Step 3: the NIPALS loop, one component at a time

Python
for a in range(A):
    u = Ya[:, int(np.argmax(Ya.var(axis=0)))]      # start from the most variable Y column
    for _ in range(500):
        w = Xa.T @ u; w /= (np.linalg.norm(w) or 1.0)   # X weights
        t = Xa @ w                                       # X scores
        q = Ya.T @ t / (t @ t)                           # Y loadings
        u_new = Ya @ q / (q @ q)                         # Y scores
        if np.linalg.norm(u_new - u) <= 1e-10 * max(np.linalg.norm(u), 1.0):
            u = u_new; break
        u = u_new
    t  = Xa @ w
    pa = Xa.T @ t / (t @ t)                              # X loadings
    q  = Ya.T @ t / (t @ t)
    Xa = Xa - np.outer(t, pa)      # deflation: subtract this component from X
    Ya = Ya - np.outer(t, q)       #                              and from Y
What NIPALS is doing
It searches for a direction w such that the projection t = Xw has maximum covariance with Y.

・PCA finds the direction of maximum variance in X alone — it never looks at Y
・PLS finds the direction of maximum covariance between X and Y — it knows the answer

The inner while loop simply projects back and forth between X and Y until it converges. After extracting a component it is subtracted from both X and Y (deflation) before the next one is extracted, which is what keeps the components orthogonal.

Step 4: regression coefficients and prediction

Python
B = W @ np.linalg.solve(P.T @ W, Q.T)      # B = W (P'W)^-1 Q'
y_hat = Xc @ B + y_mean
predicted = [classes[i] for i in np.argmax(y_hat, axis=1)]

The values in y_hat are not probabilities — they can be −0.1 or 1.3. They are regression outputs, and the usual decision rule is simply to take the largest.

Step 5: VIP

Python
ssy    = np.array([(T[:,a] @ T[:,a]) * (Q[:,a] @ Q[:,a]) for a in range(A)])
wnorm2 = np.maximum((W**2).sum(axis=0), 1e-12)
vip    = np.sqrt(p * ((W**2) / wnorm2 @ ssy) / ssy.sum())

Identical to the R formula in Chapter 17. The only difference is sweep() in R versus broadcasting in numpy.

23. Validation: LOO and exact permutation

Python
def predict(fit, x):
    yh = (x - fit["x_mean"]) @ fit["coef"] + fit["y_mean"]
    return fit["classes"][int(np.argmax(yh))]

def loocv(M, labels, A=2):
    labels = np.asarray(labels); ok = 0
    for i in range(len(labels)):
        m = np.ones(len(labels), bool); m[i] = False
        ok += predict(plsda_fit(M[m], labels[m].tolist(), A), M[i]) == labels[i]
    return ok / len(labels)
Python
from itertools import combinations
cls  = sorted(set(lab))
accs = np.array([loocv(Xbl, [cls[0] if i in idx else cls[1] for i in range(10)], 2)
                 for idx in combinations(range(10), 5)])       # all 252
obs  = loocv(Xbl, lab, 2)
print(f"p = {(accs >= obs).sum()}/{len(accs)} = {(accs >= obs).sum()/len(accs):.4f}")
Output
observed = 1.000   mean under shuffled labels = 0.426   max = 1.000
p = 2/252 = 0.0079
The only difference from the R version is syntax
R uses combn(10, 5), Python uses itertools.combinations(range(10), 5).
The 252 accuracies come out identical one by one, so of course the p-value does too.

Which is exactly the point of this tutorial: changing tools does not change the answer. If it does, one side has a bug or a different default.

Explanation: That is the fundamental unsupervised/supervised distinction. The inner NIPALS loop projects back and forth between X and Y until convergence, then deflates both to keep components orthogonal.

Yes, PLS-DA is a probabilistic model
Explanation: PLS is regression at heart. For genuine probabilities you need another layer on top, such as LDA or logistic regression on the scores.

Check the file size

Coincidence

24. Installation

What orange-spectra is

25. Preparing the data: .tab and the class column

Nine people in ten hit this error first:

It means no column has been designated as the class. Two ways to fix it:

Option A: use Orange's native .tab format (recommended)

The first three lines of a .tab file are names / types / flags, so the class column is declared in the file itself and is set up the moment you load it:

gypsum2	50.222768	43.117	…	21.004	gypsum
…
LineContentNotes

4Connect the output of Select Columns to PLS-DA
ID must go in Metas
Leave ID among the Features and Orange will hand it to PLS-DA as a variable. A string column is either ignored or coerced to a number — neither is what you want — and your VIP table will contain a "wavenumber" called ID.

Running the workflow

Bonus: plotting the loadings as spectra

Connecting Loadings to a Data Table only gives you numbers. To see them as curves, insert a Transpose:

PLS-DALoadings ▸
──▶
Transposewavenumbers from rows to columns
──▶
SpectraOrange Spectroscopy add-on

Why the transpose: the Loadings output is "one row per wavenumber, one column per component", whereas the Spectra widget wants "one row per curve, one column per wavenumber". After transposing, p1 and p2 become two overlaid curves — and because the wavenumbers are now the column names, the x-axis becomes the wavenumber axis automatically.

The payoff is that the Spectra widget has a cursor readout: hover over a peak and it tells you 1008.9, 1085.5, with no table lookup. That interactivity is something a script cannot give you.

Three rules for reading a loading curve
1. It is not a spectrum, it is a loading. The y-axis has no units and both signs are meaningful — do not read it the way you read a spectrum.
2. The sign is arbitrary. Both PLS and PCA can flip a whole component and remain exactly equivalent. So "p1 is positive at 1008" does not mean "more gypsum"; to fix the direction you must go back to the score plot and see which group sits on the positive side.
3. The plot does not label which curve is p1 and which is p2. After transposing, the curve names live in a meta column; set the Spectra widget's Menu to colour by that column.
The Status box shows training accuracy, not cross-validation
The widget's accuracy is obtained by fitting on all the data and then predicting the same data. Under p ≫ n it is almost guaranteed to be 100% — that number is not a measure of model performance.

For cross-validation, route Predictions into Orange's Test and Score. For an exact permutation test there is no ready-made widget and you must go back to R or Python (Chapters 18 and 23).
This is the one genuine capability difference between the three tools.

Orange will not fill in that last column, and neither will any other software. That is Part 1's job.

How to do it:

1Copy out the top 20–30 rows of the VIP table
2Match each against the band table in Chapter 7, allowing ±5 cm-1
3Record the assignment for the ones that match; flag the ones that do not
4For the unmatched ones, go back to the raw spectra — is there really a peak? Is it noise? Or is it present in every sample (= instrument)?
5Remove the artefact regions, re-run, and see whether the conclusion changes (sensitivity analysis)
This is where Orange earns its keep
Because it lets you change Components, change the data, change the preprocessing and see the VIP table update in seconds. Doing the same thing from a script means re-running, re-plotting and re-reading.

Explore in Orange, deliver with a script. The two are not in conflict.

Orange displays more decimal places on the wavenumber (1083.550) than the tutorial table (1083.6) — a display difference only.

What this means
The VIP table you see when you click in the Orange widget, the VIP array from this notebook, and the VIP vector from the R script are the same numbers. Not "similar".

The reason is straightforward: all three run NIPALS PLS2, all three mean-centre without scaling, and all three use the same VIP formula.
With the same algorithm, changing tools does not change the answer.

The converse holds too: if changing tools does change your answer, do not write it off as "how that tool behaves" — go and find which default differs. Nine times out of ten it is scaling, the cross-validation scheme, or SG edge handling.

Pedagogically, it is worth having students run this themselves. "Three completely different interfaces produce the same 5.718" is more convincing than any explanation.

30. The 419 artefact

VIP ranks 2, 5 and 7 are 419.2 / 422.1 / 416.4. This chapter shows they are not sample signal.

The argument is short:

1Calcite has modes at 156 / 282 / 712 / 1086 / 1435 (Chapter 4). There is no 419.
2Yet all five marble spectra show a clear peak at 419.2 (height 64.6–92.5).
3And the position is identical across samples (only marble5 reads 422.1; the rest are 419.2).
4Conclusion: 419 comes from the instrument, not the sample.
The golden rule for spotting instrument artefacts
If a band appears in a sample that chemically should not have it, it is not sample signal.

Usual suspects: laser plasma lines, filter edges, grating ghosts, fixed cosmic-ray patterns, or signal from the sample holder or slide.
The signature: the position is identical across every sample (real bands scatter by ±2–3 cm⁻¹ between samples).

Gypsum's 419 peak (mean height 200.5) is much taller than marble's (77.4) because gypsum's real ν2 at 413 sits on top of the artefact. That also explains why the measured position is 419.2 rather than the literature's 413 — the artefact drags the apparent centre upwards.

Worse: LV2 is essentially the artefact

List the six largest entries in each of the two PLS loadings:

The four largest contributions to the second latent variable all lie in the 419 artefact.

In other words LV2 is essentially an "instrument artefact component". It accounts for only 3.98% of the X variance, which is why Chapter 18 found that one component already gives 100% — LV2 is not needed for classification at all. But set Components = 2 (as most people do) and it is there, skewing the whole VIP ranking.

A check you can run immediately
If the largest loadings of some component are clustered in one narrow band and you cannot state that band's chemical assignment — assume it is instrumental until you can prove otherwise.

A genuine chemical component does not look like that. Its loadings appear on several bands of the same mineral. Look at p1: 1086, 1083, 1088, 283, 286 — all calcite, spread across two regions. An artefact has only one band, so its loadings pile up in one place.

What to do about it

  1. Report it. State the identified artefact positions in the methods or results.
  2. Run a sensitivity analysis. Drop 410–430 and re-run PCA and PLS-DA. For this dataset the conclusion does not change (1086 and 1009 are sufficient on their own), but you need to know that.
  3. Find the source. Measure a blank — a clean slide or the empty sample holder — and see whether 419 is there. If it is, the instrument. If not, suspect a contamination shared by all your samples.
Why this deserves a whole chapter
Because without Part 1's chemistry you would have written in your paper: "419 cm-1 is the key band discriminating gypsum from marble (VIP = 5.57)".

Statistically flawless. Scientifically wrong. A reviewer might not catch it, but nobody will reproduce it — on a different instrument the band is simply not there.

31. Why alabaster was excluded

The original dataset has three groups: gypsum, marble, and five spectra of alabaster. This tutorial uses only the first two. Here is why.

First a fact: alabaster is mineralogically gypsum. It is not a separate mineral; the word is a trade term for massive, fine-grained, carvable gypsum, with the same formula CaSO4·2H2O. It should look exactly like the gypsum group.

Metricalabastergypsummarble
S/N at 1008 (sulfate ν1)2.3 (1.5–3.3)16.7 (10.8–25.3)1.9
S/N at 1086 (carbonate ν1)——16.4 (9.6–23.9)
fluorescence background (mean ALS baseline)175.665.593.3
identifiable mineral bands063

The detection threshold is S/N ≥ 3. Only one of the five alabaster spectra even reaches 3.3; the rest are below 3. Its fluorescence background is 2.7 times that of the gypsum group, and the signal is drowned.

How to write this correctly
You cannot write "alabaster contains no sulfate".
You write: "Under the present measurement conditions the alabaster samples exhibited a fluorescence background strong enough that the sulfate ν1 band did not reach the detection threshold (S/N 1.5–3.3); their mineral composition could not be confirmed by Raman spectroscopy."

"Not detected" is not "not present". The gap between those two sentences is the gap between what the data said and what you wanted it to say.

What happens if you keep it as a third class

We actually ran it. Three-class PLS-DA gives leave-one-out accuracy 100% with permutation p = 0.002. It looks perfect.

But alabaster versus gypsum — the same mineral — is also 100%, p = 0.006. And the top three VIP entries are the instrument artefact and "whether 1008 was drowned by fluorescence".

What the model separates perfectly is not two minerals. It is two measurement qualities.

This is confounding, not an algorithm problem. Switch to SVM, random forest or deep learning and you get the same answer, because the problem is in the data.

So: should you use poor-quality data?
Not as a class in a model. But keep it as teaching material.

・As a class → you obtain a beautiful-looking model that has learned instrument conditions
・As a quality-control case → it is the single most valuable group of spectra in the whole dataset

The remedy is a return to the bench, not a change of algorithm: measure a different spot, lower the laser power and lengthen the integration (high power dehydrates gypsum and pushes ν1 from 1008 towards 1015), or move to a 1064 nm laser to avoid exciting the fluorescence. The literature also offers near-infrared reflectance as an alternative, using the 1440–1540 nm triplet to separate gypsum from marble.

32. p ≫ n: the floor on accuracy and the floor on p

10 samples, 664 variables. Two things you must know in the small-sample, high-dimensional regime.

Floor one: shuffled labels already score 42.6%

Shuffle the labels and re-run: mean accuracy 0.426, maximum 1.000, with a substantial fraction landing between 0.6 and 0.8.

Which means: if your model reaches 70%, you have demonstrated nothing. That sits comfortably inside the random range.

Floor two: p cannot go below 0.0079

Of the 252 assignments, exactly two reach 100%: the true labelling, and the one with both labels swapped (the model learns the reversed mapping and scores identically).

pmin = 2 / C(10,5) = 2 / 252 = 0.0079
Per groupTotal assignments C(2k,k)Lowest possible p
4 + 4700.029
5 + 5 (this tutorial)2520.0079
6 + 69240.0022
7 + 734320.00058
Read this table while designing the experiment, not after analysing it
If your journal or reviewer expects p < 0.001, you need at least six spectra per group.
A four-versus-four design cannot even reach p < 0.01 — however immaculate your signal.

This is not a statistical subtlety, it is arithmetic. Measuring two more samples costs far less than discovering after the analysis that your p-value is capped.

Why exact enumeration rather than random permutation

The usual approach is to shuffle 499 or 999 times. But with only 252 possibilities, 499 draws must repeat, and the sampling itself adds uncertainty.

When the sample is small, enumerate everything: it is faster, it is exact, and the p-value is a definite number rather than an estimate. combn() in R, itertools.combinations() in Python — one line either way.

33. Something nobody mentions: uncalibrated intensity response

Compare the measured peak positions against the literature and the wavenumber calibration is excellent:

LiteratureMeasuredDifference
gypsum ν1 10081009.3+1.3
calcite ν1 10861086.00.0
calcite lattice 282286.4+4.4
calcite ν4 712709.2−2.8

The main bands are within 0–1.3 cm-1. Peak positions can be trusted.

Relative intensities cannot:

RatioMeasuredExpected
I(1009) / I(419) gypsum0.65well above 1 (1008 is gypsum's strongest band)
I(1086) / I(282) marble1.05clearly above 1 (1086 is calcite's strongest band)

Both groups show the same bias — relatively weak at the high-wavenumber end. That is not the sample; it is an uncalibrated instrument response, since both grating efficiency and CCD quantum efficiency fall off with wavenumber.

What it does and does not affect
Unaffected: peak identification, PCA, PLS-DA, VIP ranking — provided every sample was measured on the same instrument with the same settings, the bias is common to all of them.

Affected: anything based on peak height ratios — semi-quantification, mixing proportions, crystallinity indices, comparison across instruments.

To correct it, measure a white-light standard (NIST SRM 2241/2242) once and divide the response curve out. You may also choose not to correct it — but then state in the methods that no intensity calibration was performed, so readers know your intensity ratios do not transfer between instruments.

Incidentally, this also partly explains why the 419 artefact looks so prominent: it sits in the region where the instrument responds best.

34. Error list and pre-submission checklist

#MistakeConsequenceHow to avoid it

Pre-submission checklist

  • Laser wavelength, power, integration time, accumulations, objective
  • Wavenumber calibration method (silicon 520.7? polystyrene 1001.4?)
  • Whether an intensity-response calibration was done (say so even if not)
  • Crop range and the reason for it
  • Baseline method and all its parameters (ALS: λ, p, iterations)
  • Smoothing method and parameters (SG: window, polynomial order, edge handling)
  • Whether SNV / derivatives were used, and why
  • PCA center / scale settings
  • PLS-DA component count and how it was chosen
  • Cross-validation scheme, and whether preprocessing / variable selection sat inside the loop
  • Permutation test: number of permutations (or a note that it was exhaustive), observed value, null mean, p
  • High-VIP wavenumbers with their chemical assignments; explain any that do not match
  • Instrument artefacts identified
  • S/N per group and the detection threshold applied
  • Random seed; software and package versions
  • Where the data and code can be obtained
One last thing
What this tutorial is really about is not where the PCA or PLS-DA buttons are — you can learn all three tools in ten minutes.

It is about this: when the model hands you 100% accuracy, knowing what to be suspicious of.
