Knowing what to be suspicious of when the model hands you 100% accuracy
How to tune preprocessing parameters
Explanation: All three tools can be learned in ten minutes. The hard part is knowing when not to believe your own model — and Raman's advantage is that every peak can be checked against the question 'what bond is moving there?'.

Part 7 — Preprocessing with established packagesFour chapters. Having hand-written it once, switch to the packages — and to the three defaults that bite

35. Why the first six parts were hand-written

The ALS, Savitzky–Golay and SNV code in Parts 1–6 is all hand-written — under forty lines in total. Not because there are no packages, but because you have to know what those forty lines compute before you can judge whether a package's defaults are right for your data.

Now turn it around. In practice this is what you would write:

R
install.packages(c("baseline", "prospectr"))

bc    <- baseline::baseline(X, method = "als", lambda = 4, p = 0.01)
Xcorr <- baseline::getCorrected(bc)
Xsg   <- prospectr::savitzkyGolay(Xcorr, m = 0, p = 3, w = 9)
Xsnv  <- prospectr::standardNormalVariate(Xsg)
Python
pip install pybaselines

from pybaselines.whittaker import asls
from scipy.signal import savgol_filter

Xcorr = np.array([y - asls(y, lam=1e4, p=0.01)[0] for y in X])
Xsg   = savgol_filter(Xcorr, 9, 3, axis=1)
Xsnv  = (Xsg - Xsg.mean(1, keepdims=True)) / Xsg.std(1, ddof=1, keepdims=True)

Four lines instead of forty, and battle-tested against edge cases by a few thousand users. For real analysis, use the packages.

So why read this part?
Because three defaults will quietly change your result on the way across, and none of them raises an error:

1. In R's baseline package, lambda is log10. Your hand-written 1e4 becomes 1010000.
2. prospectr::savitzkyGolay discards 4 points at each end. Forget to trim the wavenumber axis and the whole VIP table shifts by 12 cm-1.
3. Without delta.wav / delta, a derivative is "per data point", not "per cm-1".

None of the three crashes. Chapter 37 quantifies each one.

36. R: baseline and prospectr

baseline

baseline (Liland & Mevik) collects a dozen baseline algorithms behind one interface; als is only one of them:

R
bc <- baseline::baseline(X, method = "als", lambda = 4, p = 0.01, maxit = 20)

baseline::getBaseline(bc)    # the baseline itself
baseline::getCorrected(bc)   # the corrected spectra
plot(bc)                     # built-in diagnostic plot

# other methods worth knowing:
#   "irls"        iteratively reweighted, robust against curved backgrounds
#   "modpolyfit"  iterative polynomial (Lieber & Mahadevan-Jansen -- the one
#                 most often cited in the Raman literature)
#   "rollingBall" rolling ball, fast

Three details that will catch you:

  1. spectra must be a matrix. For a single spectrum write X[1, , drop = FALSE], or baseline() stops with an error.
  2. Spectra go in rows — the layout used throughout this repo, and the opposite of some other software.
  3. lambda is a power of ten. lambda = 4 is what equals the hand-written lambda = 1e4.

prospectr

prospectr (Stevens & Ramirez-Lopez) is the Swiss army knife of chemometric preprocessing. Written for NIR, but it works just as well on Raman:

R
prospectr::savitzkyGolay(X, m = 0, p = 3, w = 9)   # smoothing
prospectr::savitzkyGolay(X, m = 1, p = 3, w = 9, delta.wav = 2.4863)  # 1st derivative
prospectr::standardNormalVariate(X)                # SNV
prospectr::detrend(X, wav = wn)                    # SNV + quadratic detrend
prospectr::msc(X)                                  # multiplicative scatter correction
prospectr::continuumRemoval(X, wav = wn)           # convex-hull background removal
prospectr::binning(X, bins = 100)                  # dimension reduction
prospectr::resample(X, wav = wn, new.wav = seq(150, 1800, 2))  # onto an even grid
resample is especially useful for Raman
The wavenumber axis in this tutorial is not evenly spaced (about 3.0 cm-1 per point at the low end, 2.3 at the high end). The Savitzky–Golay derivation assumes even sampling — strictly, SG on an uneven axis is an approximation.

On this data the error is invisible (all three tools agree to 10-13) because the spacing varies by under 1% inside a 9-point window. But if your spectra span a much wider range, or you are mixing FT-Raman with dispersive data, resample() onto an even grid before the SG step.

37. The three defaults that bite

Trap #1: is lambda 10⁴ or 4?

One AsLS algorithm, three implementations, two conventions:

implementationargumentdefaultmeaning
hand-written herelambda1e4linear
pybaselines.whittaker.aslslam1e6linear
baseline::baseline.alslambda6log10 → 10⁶

Paste the hand-written 1e4 into R's lambda and you have asked for 1010000. R does not complain; it hands you a straight line.

Package defaults (lambda = 6, p = 0.05) against aligned parameters (lambda = 4, p = 0.01):

Output
hand(1e4)  vs  baseline::als(lambda=4, p=.01) : RMSD 0.000e+00   <= identical
hand(1e4)  vs  baseline::als(lambda=6, p=.05) : RMSD   6.6413 counts

1008 cm-1 peak height: hand 143.1 | lambda=4 143.1 | lambda=6 (default) 134.5  -> 6.0% apart

The classification does not change — 1008 is still 1008 and the VIP ranking still looks the same. But the peak height moved by 6%. If you intend to use peak heights semi-quantitatively, or report a band-area ratio, that is not a rounding error.

Trap #2: Savitzky–Golay edges

The interior coefficients are identical in all three implementations (agreement to 10-13). The difference is confined to the 4 points at each end:

implementationedge handlingoutput length
hand-written herereplicate the end points664 (unchanged)
scipy.signal.savgol_filterpolynomial extrapolation (mode='interp')664 (unchanged)
prospectr::savitzkyGolaydiscarded656 (w−1 fewer)
This one silently ruins your VIP table
X goes from 664 columns to 656, but wn still has 664 entries. When you map VIP scores back to wavenumbers, column i gets labelled wn[i] instead of wn[5+i] — the whole table shifts by 4 points, which on this data is 12.0 cm-1.

1008 reads as 1020. There is nothing at 1020, so you start hunting for an unknown species.

The fix: wn_sg <- wn[5:(length(wn) - 4)], once per SG call. A smoothing-plus-first-derivative chain takes 664 down to 648.

Trap #3: the units of a derivative

savgol_filter(..., deriv=1) defaults to delta=1.0; prospectr does nothing unless you pass delta.wav. Either way the result is change per data point, not per cm-1.

Output
without delta.wav  max|d1| = 49.9192   (per POINT)
with    delta.wav  max|d1| = 20.0773   (per cm-1, a factor of 2.4863 = mean step)

This has no effect on classification — every variable is multiplied by the same constant, so PCA directions, PLS-DA scores and VIP rankings are all unchanged. But the moment you report a derivative value in a paper, or compare against data from another instrument, the units have to be cm-1.

38. The one without a trap, and how to write the methods section

SNV: exact agreement

prospectr::standardNormalVariate divides by n−1, the same as R's sd(). The hand-written version uses sd(), so the two are bit-for-bit equal (8.9×10-16, pure floating-point rounding).

Python needs more care: numpy's .std() defaults to ddof=0.

Python
Y.std(1, keepdims=True)              # ddof=0 -- does NOT match R
Y.std(1, ddof=1, keepdims=True)      # matches prospectr / R's sd()

Over 664 points the two differ by √(664/663) = 1.000754, i.e. 0.075% — invisible. Run binning() down to 20 wavenumbers first and the gap becomes 2.5%.

The whole chain, package version

R
STEP  <- mean(diff(wn))                                    # 2.4863

bc    <- baseline::baseline(X, method = "als", lambda = 4, p = 0.01, maxit = 20)
Xcorr <- baseline::getCorrected(bc)                        # 10 x 664
Xsg   <- prospectr::savitzkyGolay(Xcorr, m = 0, p = 3, w = 9)      # 10 x 656
wn_sg <- wn[5:(length(wn) - 4)]                            # 664 -> 656
Xsnv  <- prospectr::standardNormalVariate(Xsg)
Xd1   <- prospectr::savitzkyGolay(Xsnv, m = 1, p = 3, w = 9, delta.wav = STEP)
wn_d1 <- wn_sg[5:(length(wn_sg) - 4)]                      # 656 -> 648

stopifnot(ncol(Xd1) == length(wn_d1))    # <- add this line after every step
One stopifnot buys back a night of debugging
Put stopifnot(ncol(X) == length(wn)) after every preprocessing step. It fails the moment the dimensions stop matching, rather than three hours into a literature search for whatever is supposed to be at 1020 cm-1.

Part 7 · Quiz

Q1.What smoothing parameter does R's <code>baseline::baseline.als(lambda = 6)</code> actually use?
6
10⁶ = 1000000
6 × 10⁴
It is chosen automatically from the data
Explanation: The source reads DD <- .create_DD(m) * 10^lambda. lambda is an exponent. pybaselines' lam is the linear value — two different conventions for the same algorithm.
Q2.You paste the hand-written <code>lambda = 1e4</code> straight into <code>baseline::baseline.als</code>. What happens?
An error; the script stops
It runs, but the baseline is essentially a straight line (you asked for 10^10000 smoothness)
It is silently corrected to 4
The result matches the hand-written version
Explanation: No error — that is what makes it dangerous. An enormous lambda drives the second-difference penalty to its limit, the baseline degenerates to a straight line, and your spectra look 'corrected' while nothing was removed.
Q3.<code>prospectr::savitzkyGolay(X, m = 0, p = 3, w = 9)</code> is given 664 columns. How many come back?
664
656
672
660
Explanation: Valid convolution: (w−1)/2 = 4 points are dropped from each end, so w−1 = 8 columns are lost. scipy's savgol_filter pads instead and preserves length — the single most confusable difference between the two.
Q4.Following on: you forget to trim the axis and label the VIP table with the original <code>wn</code>. Where does the 1008 cm⁻¹ band appear?
1008 — no effect
around 996
around 1020
at a random offset
Explanation: The whole table shifts by 4 points, which on this data is +12.0 cm⁻¹. There is no known band near 1020, so you end up chasing a species that does not exist.
Q5.Why does omitting <code>delta.wav</code> leave the PLS-DA classification unchanged?
Because derivatives are useless anyway
Because it multiplies every variable by the same constant, changing no direction or ranking
Because PLS-DA standardises internally
Because the error is too small to matter
Explanation: Multiplying X by a constant c leaves PCA eigenvector directions, PLS weight directions and relative VIP rankings untouched. It only matters the moment you quote an absolute derivative value.
Q6.How does <code>numpy</code>'s <code>Y.std(1)</code> differ from <code>prospectr::standardNormalVariate</code>?
numpy defaults to ddof=0; prospectr uses n−1
numpy works column-wise, prospectr row-wise
numpy does not subtract the mean first
There is no difference
Explanation: Both work row-wise and both centre first; only the denominator differs. 0.075% over 664 points, but 2.5% after binning to 20 wavenumbers. R's sd() is n−1 already, so the R version never hits this.
Q7.Strictly speaking, what is a Savitzky–Golay filter applied to an unevenly spaced wavenumber axis?
Exactly correct
An approximation — the SG derivation assumes even sampling
Completely invalid; you must always resample first
A problem only for derivatives
Explanation: The coefficients come from a least-squares fit on an even grid. Here the spacing varies by under 1% within a 9-point window, so the error is invisible; over a much wider range, resample() onto an even grid first.
Q8.A methods section says &ldquo;ALS baseline correction was applied&rdquo;. What is wrong with it?
Nothing, that is the standard phrasing
It gives neither implementation nor parameters — and lambda alone follows two different conventions
It should cite a different algorithm
ALS should not be used on Raman data
Explanation: Write it as: pybaselines 1.2.1, whittaker.asls, lam = 1e4, p = 0.01, 15 iterations. Otherwise nobody can reproduce it — the same 'lambda = 6' differs by a factor of 100 between two common packages.

Part 8 — External validation: testing your model on somebody else's dataFive chapters. Same mineral, different laboratory, different excitation — does the model still recognise it?

39. Leave-one-out cannot demonstrate generalisation

The PLS-DA in Chapter 18 scored 100% under leave-one-out, and the exact permutation test in Chapter 32 gave p = 0.0079. Those two numbers establish that the model is trustworthy within these ten spectra. What they do not establish is whether it still recognises gypsum on a different instrument, in a different laboratory, at a different excitation wavelength.

Confusing the two is the single most common reason a chemometrics paper comes back from review.

Internal validation (LOO, bootstrap, permutation)
Answers: within my data, is this separation a fluke?
Every sample shares one instrument, one calibration, one set of operator habits. Leave-one-out does not break any of those apart, because they are still present in every fold.
External validation (independent samples)
Answers: did the model learn chemistry, or my machine's quirks?
The only way to find out is to project samples the model has never seen and that came from somewhere else.

The external data used here is somebody else's published open dataset:

Data source
A. Martínez-Hernández, M. Oujja, M. Sanz, E. Carrasco, V. Detalle, M. Castillejo, “Analysis of heritage stones and model wall paintings by pulsed laser excitation of Raman, laser-induced fluorescence and laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy signals with a hybrid system”, Journal of Cultural Heritage 32 (2018) 1–8. doi:10.1016/j.culher.2018.02.004

The dataset itself is deposited separately on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0:
doi:10.5281/zenodo.3532931 (Dataset, 2019-11-08).
Funded by EU IPERION-CH (H2020, Project 654028).

The article itself is not open access (© 2018 Elsevier Masson SAS, All rights reserved) — the data may be redistributed, the PDF may not. Chapter 43 works through what that means for GitHub.

What makes this dataset a good external test is that almost every condition differs:

this tutorialJ. Cult. Herit. 32 (2018)
excitationcontinuous-wave dispersive355 nm pulsed (Nd:YAG 3rd harmonic, 17 ns, 10 Hz)
detectorCCDtime-gated ICCD (Andor DH-501, delay 0 / gate 50 ns)
spectrograph—Bentham TMc300, 0.30 m, 1200 lines/mm, 50 μm slit
accumulationssingle125
techniqueRaman onlyhybrid LIF-Raman (fluorescence-dominated, Raman riding on top)
samplesgypsum, marble, alabaster × 5 eachalabaster, gypsum, limestone, white marble

If the model still gets it right under those conditions, whatever it learned was not an instrument signature.

40. Read the files before you model them: three traps

The first thing to do with somebody else's open data is not to run a model. It is to work out what each file actually is. This dataset has three ways to get that wrong.

Trap 1: Alaba35501–05 are not five replicate spectra

The filenames look like five samples. They are five grating positions from a single measurement, tiled end to end:

filewavelength (nm)converted (cm-1)
Alaba35501362.70 – 415.05598 – 4076 (contains the fingerprint region)
Alaba35502415.96 – 463.854129 – 6610
Alaba35503463.74 – 517.666605 – 8851
Alaba35504517.47 – 565.438844 – 10484
Alaba35505565.16 – 619.7810475 – 12034

Each segment spans about 52 nm — and the paper says so explicitly: the 1200 lines/mm grating provides “a spectral coverage of 50 […] nm […] in the 250–650 nm region”. Five segments of 50 nm cover 362–620 nm exactly.

So there is one independent alabaster spectrum. Files 35502–05 are the 4000–12000 cm-1 fluorescence tail — that is LIF, not Raman.

Trap 2: Whitemarble355-001 and -003 are the same file

Shell
$ md5sum Whitemarble355-001.dat Whitemarble355-003.dat
0575ff0c7e0149d09296cbe6e187667b  Whitemarble355-001.dat
0575ff0c7e0149d09296cbe6e187667b  Whitemarble355-003.dat

Byte-for-byte identical. Treating them as two independent samples means manufacturing a replicate. Run md5sum on any dataset you did not produce yourself.

Trap 3: the x axis is nanometres, not Raman shift

The first column of each .dat is wavelength. You have to convert it:

Raman shift (cm-1) = 107/λex(nm) − 107/λ(nm)

And λex cannot be copied from the metadata — which is the next chapter.

Independent spectra usable in the fingerprint region: four
One alabaster, one gypsum, one limestone, one white marble.
That number drives every design decision that follows — a class with n = 1 cannot go into the training set. It can only be projected as an external sample. Chapter 42 explains why.

41. A 46 cm⁻¹ error in the wavelength axis, and how to prove it is one

The metadata spreadsheet gives the excitation wavelength as 355. Convert with that number and the four ν1 bands land at:

Output
Alaba35501              963.5 cm-1     (SO4 v1 should be at 1008)
YESO35507               955.0 cm-1     (SO4 v1 should be at 1008)
CALIZA355001           1028.0 cm-1     (CO3 v1 should be at 1086)
Whitemarble355-001     1058.7 cm-1     (CO3 v1 should be at 1086)

Every one is 27–58 cm-1 too low. The reason is that “355 nm” is the nominal third harmonic of a Nd:YAG; the real output is close to 354.4 nm. Around 355 nm, a 0.5 nm wavelength error is a 40 cm-1 shift.

Why this is not circular reasoning

“Derive λex from the known band positions, then declare the band positions correct” sounds like arguing in a circle. Three independent checks say it is not.

Check 1: the authors state the positions they measured. Section 3.1 reports 197, 313, 415, 494, 619, 671, 1008 and 1135 cm-1 for alabaster and gypsum, and 154, 281, 711, 1085, 1445 and 1744 cm-1 for limestone and marble. In other words — 963 / 955 / 1028 / 1059, the values you get by taking 355.0 literally, do not even match the authors' own numbers. That is evidence entirely independent of us.
Check 2: do the back-derived values cluster by mineral? The sulfate pair averages 354.387 nm, the carbonate pair 354.464 nm — a gap of 77 pm. A wrong assignment (calling SO4 a CO3) would force the two groups 979 pm apart. An order of magnitude difference.
Check 3: swapping the assignments blows up. Assign every band to the other species and the standard deviation of the four λex values jumps from 0.169 nm to 1.187 nm — you would have to assume they ran four different lasers at once.

Finally, everything downstream uses a single shared constant, λex = 354.425 nm, with no per-file fitting. With that one constant the four bands have an RMS residual of 11.7 cm-1:

Output
file                       observed  assigned  residual
Alaba35501.dat               1009.2      1008      +1.2
YESO35507.dat                1000.7      1008      -7.3
CALIZA355001.dat            1073.7      1086     -12.3
Whitemarble355-001.dat      1104.4      1086     +18.4
                                    RMS = 11.7 cm-1

What should that residual be compared against? The instrumental bandwidth:

ν1 band FWHM
this tutorial, gypsum 100812.5 cm-1
this tutorial, marble 108612.2 cm-1
JCH alabaster / gypsum / limestone / marble34 / 48 / 43 / 53 cm-1

An 11.7 cm-1 residual is well inside one resolution element. That a single constant puts all four bands back where they belong is itself the evidence.

The real lesson of this chapter
Numbers in metadata are nominal, not measured.
“355 nm”, “532 nm”, “785 nm” are product labels. The actual output wavelength has to be calibrated against a standard (silicon 520.7, cyclohexane, polystyrene) or against a known band in the sample itself.

Your own data is no different — the 419 cm-1 artefact in Chapter 30 is the same class of problem: an instrument state nobody checked. The only difference is that one of them gets caught by VIP and the other does not.

42. PCA and PLS-DA: projecting the external samples

Nineteen spectra (our 15 plus the published 4), on a shared window of 620–1790 cm-1 (the published data stops at 598, so calcite's 156/282 lattice modes and gypsum's 413/493 ν2 bands are simply unavailable), 5 cm-1 per point, identical preprocessing.

PCA

scenarioPC1PC2instrument gap ÷ mineral gap (on PC1)
355.0 nm taken literally37.4%26.8%0.77
calibrated, 354.425 nm46.5%26.9%0.17
calibrated + resolution matched51.0%34.5%0.18

Taken literally, “which instrument” is almost as big a effect on PC1 as “which mineral” (0.77). All four published spectra pile up on the negative side of PC1 regardless of mineralogy — the clustering is by laboratory.

After calibration PC1 becomes a clean sulfate-versus-carbonate axis and the instrument effect drops to a sixth of the mineral effect.

The instrument difference did not vanish — it moved to PC2
After calibration the four published spectra all sit low on PC2 (−5 to −11) while our fifteen scatter around zero. PC2 is the “different instrument” axis.

That is a good outcome, not a bad one. The confounder has been isolated onto a component you can see, rather than smeared through PC1 and tangled up with the chemistry. Once you can see it, you can decide whether to use it.

PLS-DA trained on our ten spectra only

The design matters: only our own 5 gypsum + 5 marble train the model (2 components). The four published spectra take no part in training and are projected in as external samples. Training-set leave-one-out is 10/10 in all three scenarios.

sampletruth355.0 literalcalibrated
Alaba35501 (alabaster)sulfate✗ marble (ygyp 0.46)✓ gypsum (0.96)
YESO35507 (gypsum)sulfate✓ gypsum (0.51)✓ gypsum (0.92)
CALIZA355001 (limestone)carbonate✗ gypsum (0.84)✓ marble (0.82)
Whitemarble355-001carbonate✓ marble (0.46)✓ marble (0.86)
2 / 44 / 4
Read the y values, not just right-versus-wrong
In the literal column, three of the four predictions fall between 0.46 and 0.51 — the model is tossing a coin and happens to get two right.
The one prediction it is confident about (CALIZA, 0.84) is wrong.

A confident wrong answer is far more dangerous than a coin toss. Accuracy alone says 50% and reads as “weak model”; the y values reveal that the real fault is upstream, in the axis of the incoming data.

An answer to the question left open in Chapter 31

Our own five alabaster specimens are classified as gypsum 5/5 in all three scenarios. The published alabaster is likewise classified as gypsum, with 0.96 confidence, once calibrated. And the authors themselves report, in section 3.1, that alabaster and gypsum show the same set of SO42− bands.

Two laboratories, two instruments, two excitation wavelengths, plus the authors' own band assignments —
three independent routes to the same answer: both alabasters are gypsum-based.

Chapter 31 argued that alabaster and gypsum are the same mineral and dropped the class. The evidence then was five specimens of our own. Now there is independent corroboration. That is what external validation buys you — it tests not only the model but your reading of the material.

43. References, data licensing, and what to check before pushing to GitHub

References

Castillejo, “Analysis of heritage stones and model wall paintings by pulsed laser excitation of Raman, laser-induced fluorescence and laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy signals with a hybrid system”, Journal of Cultural Heritage 32 (2018) 1–8. doi:10.1016/j.culher.2018.02.004
  2. A. Martínez-Hernández et al., Analysis of heritage stones and model wall paintings… [Dataset]. Zenodo, 2019-11-08. doi:10.5281/zenodo.3532931. Licensed CC BY 4.0.
  3. RRUFF Project database of Raman spectroscopy — rruff.info
  4. ENS Lyon, Handbook of Raman Spectra — geologie-lyon.fr/Raman
  5. P.H.C. Eilers, H.F.M. Boelens, Baseline Correction with Asymmetric Least Squares Smoothing, 2005.
  6. A. Savitzky, M.J.E. Golay, Anal. Chem. 36 (1964) 1627–1639.

Licensing: two things that must be kept apart

itemlicencemay it go on GitHub?
the Zenodo dataset
.dat / .xlsx		CC BY 4.0Yes, with attribution
the Elsevier article PDF
1-s2.0-…-main.pdf		© 2018 Elsevier Masson SAS
All rights reserved		No
The usual misconception
“Supplementary data always carries the same licence as the article” — it does not.

This particular article is paywalled (ScienceDirect serves it at /article/abs/, and the copyright line reads All rights reserved), yet the authors separately deposited the data on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0. Different licences.

The reverse happens too: an open-access article whose supplementary data carries no explicit licence at all. Check each one separately, every time.

What CC BY 4.0 actually requires

It is not “do whatever you like”. The BY stands for attribution, and there are four obligations:

  1. Credit the original authors (A. Martínez-Hernández, M. Oujja, M. Sanz, E. Carrasco, V. Detalle, M. Castillejo)
  2. State the licence and link to its full text
  3. Provide a link to the original source (the Zenodo DOI)
  4. If you modified it, say what you changed (we converted the wavenumber axis, resampled, and used only four files)

In practice: put a DATA_SOURCES.md in the repo, and block PDFs in .gitignore:

Shell
# .gitignore
*.pdf
1-s2.0-*

Pre-push checklist

1. No publisher PDFs. git ls-files '*.pdf' should return nothing. If one was ever committed, deleting the file is not enough — it is still in the history.
2. Third-party data has a DATA_SOURCES.md. Authors, licence, DOI, and what you changed.
3. Your own material is licensed too. This repo: code MIT, tutorial text and figures CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
4. Derived data is labelled as derived. We ship a converted and resampled CSV, not the original .dat files, and the header says so.
5. Reproducing a figure from the paper needs permission. Every figure here was recomputed and redrawn from the CC BY data — legally that is a completely different act from scanning the paper's figure.
So is the tutorial itself fine on GitHub?
Yes. With the PDF excluded, the repo contains:
• fifteen spectra we measured — our own work
• CC BY 4.0 open data, attributed — redistribution permitted
• every figure recomputed and redrawn from the above
• facts and numbers cited from the paper (band positions, instrument specifications) — facts are not copyrightable, and the source is fully cited

The PDF is the only thing that cannot go.

Part 8 · Quiz

Q1.Leave-one-out 100% and a permutation p of 0.0079. What has that established?
The model will work on any instrument
That within these ten spectra the separation is not a fluke — nothing about changing instruments
That the sample size is sufficient
That the band assignments are correct
Explanation: Every fold still shares the same instrument, calibration and operator habits; leave-one-out cannot break those apart. Generalisation can only be answered with samples from a different source.
Q2.What are Alaba35501 through Alaba35505?
Five alabaster samples
Five repeat measurements
Five grating windows of one measurement, tiled end to end
Five different preprocessing treatments
Explanation: Each spans about 52 nm, exactly the 50 nm coverage the paper quotes for its 1200 lines/mm grating. Five of them cover 362–620 nm. So there is one independent alabaster spectrum, and only 35501 reaches the fingerprint region.
Q3.What is the first thing to do with an open dataset you did not produce?
Run PCA
Run md5sum for duplicates and establish what each file actually is
Plot it
Baseline-correct it
Explanation: Whitemarble355-001 and -003 in this dataset are byte-for-byte identical. Counting them as two samples manufactures a replicate and inflates cross-validation.
Q4.The metadata says 355 nm, yet converting with it puts every band about 46 cm⁻¹ too low. Why?
The data is wrong
'355' is the nominal Nd:YAG third harmonic; the real output is nearer 354.4 nm
The Raman shift formula is wrong
The samples are impure
Explanation: Near 355 nm a 0.5 nm wavelength error is roughly 40 cm⁻¹. A nominal wavelength is not a measured one — the same class of problem as the 419 cm⁻¹ artefact in Chapter 30: an instrument state nobody checked.
Q5.'Derive λex from known band positions, then declare the positions correct.' Which check best defeats the charge of circularity?
The residual is small
The authors state in the text that they measured 1008 and 1085 cm⁻¹ — the literal 355.0 conversion does not even match their own numbers
There are four files
The PLS-DA got it right
Explanation: The authors' reported positions are evidence entirely independent of our analysis. The other two checks (back-derived values not clustering by mineral; swapping assignments inflating the sd from 0.169 to 1.187 nm) are internal-consistency arguments — strong, but the paper's text is external.
Q6.After calibration, where did the 'different instrument' effect go in the PCA?
It vanished
It is still on PC1
Onto PC2 — the four published spectra all sit low there
Into the residual
Explanation: The confounder is isolated onto a component you can see, rather than tangled up with the chemistry on PC1. Visible is far more useful than gone.
Q7.The literal-355.0 PLS-DA scores 2/4. Why is that worse than a plain 50% accuracy?
Because the sample size is small
Because three predictions sit at 0.46–0.51 (coin-tossing) and the only confident one, 0.84, is wrong
Because there was no cross-validation
Because no permutation test was run
Explanation: A confident wrong answer is more dangerous than a coin toss. Accuracy alone reads as 'weak model'; the y values show the real fault is upstream, in the axis of the incoming data.
Q8.The PDF says © 2018 Elsevier, All rights reserved; the same data on Zenodo says CC BY 4.0. What may go on GitHub?
Both
Neither
The data only, not the PDF
The PDF only
Explanation: An article and its dataset can carry different licences, and each must be checked separately. The data is CC BY 4.0 (credit the authors, name the licence, link the DOI, and state what you changed); the PDF is fully reserved. If a PDF was ever committed, deleting it is not enough — it remains in the history.

Raman Analysis of Gypsum and Marble — data: 5 gypsum + 5 marble spectra, 2048 points over 77.4–3806.1 cm-1, cropped to 150–1800 (664 points).

Every number and figure was generated by running r/rock_raman_tutorial.R (R 4.3.3, pls 2.8.3) and python/rock_raman_tutorial.ipynb (numpy 2.4, scipy 1.17), random seed 20260814. The Orange sections use the PLS-DA widget from orange-spectra 0.5.0.

Band assignments follow standard mineral Raman references; see RRUFF and the ENS Lyon Handbook of Raman Spectra.
